summary.text: At \(n=473165\), the Sierpiński number \(5292270077783=a(n)+4\) lies strictly between \(a(n)=5292270077779\) and \(a(n)+28=5292270077807\). Its Sierpiński property follows from a period-\(48\) covering: for every exponent residue modulo \(48\), one of \(3,5,7,17,97,257,673\) is a proper divisor of \(5292270077783\cdot2^m+1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810n.
\]
Recall that a Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(k>1\) such that, for every positive integer \(m\), the number
\[
k2^m+1
\]
is composite.

We disprove the conjecture by taking
\[
n=473{,}165.
\]
At this index, direct arithmetic gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(473{,}165)
&=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810\cdot473{,}165\\
&=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}779.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consider the integer
\[
K=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783=a(473{,}165)+4.
\]
We will prove that \(K\) is itself a Sierpiński number. Since
\[
a(473{,}165)<K<a(473{,}165)+28,
\]
this will exhibit a Sierpiński number strictly between the two claimed consecutive Sierpiński numbers.

First, \(K\) is odd and is greater than \(1\). It remains to show that \(K2^m+1\) is composite for every positive integer \(m\). We do so with a covering argument of period \(48\).

The possible divisors used in the covering are
\[
3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 17,\ 97,\ 257,\ 673.
\]
For every one of these integers \(p\),
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
For completeness, the exact divisions of \(2^{48}=281{,}474{,}976{,}710{,}656\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p&2^{48}\text{ written as }pq+1\\ \hline
3   &3\cdot93{,}824{,}992{,}236{,}885+1\\
5   &5\cdot56{,}294{,}995{,}342{,}131+1\\
7   &7\cdot40{,}210{,}710{,}958{,}665+1\\
17  &17\cdot16{,}557{,}351{,}571{,}215+1\\
97  &97\cdot2{,}901{,}803{,}883{,}615+1\\
257 &257\cdot1{,}095{,}233{,}372{,}415+1\\
673 &673\cdot418{,}239{,}192{,}735+1.
\end{array}
\]
Consequently, if \(m=48q+r\), where \(0\le r<48\), then for each of these possible divisors,
\[
2^m=(2^{48})^q2^r\equiv2^r\pmod p.
\]
Thus it suffices to select, for each possible residue \(r=m\bmod48\), a number \(p\) from the displayed set for which
\[
K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]

The needed residues of \(K\) are given by the following exact divisions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=3\cdot1{,}764{,}090{,}025{,}927+2,\\
K&=5\cdot1{,}058{,}454{,}015{,}556+3,\\
K&=7\cdot756{,}038{,}582{,}540+3,\\
K&=17\cdot311{,}310{,}004{,}575+8,\\
K&=97\cdot54{,}559{,}485{,}337+94,\\
K&=257\cdot20{,}592{,}490{,}575+8,\\
K&=673\cdot7{,}863{,}699{,}966+665.
\end{aligned}
\]
The complete covering of the 48 residue classes is as follows.

1. **Even residues.** If \(r\) is even, use \(p=3\). Since \(2^2\equiv1\pmod3\), we have \(2^r\equiv1\pmod3\). Also \(K\equiv2\pmod3\), so
\[
K2^r+1\equiv2\cdot1+1=3\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
This covers all 24 even residues.

2. **Residues congruent to \(3\pmod4\).** These are
\[
3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35,39,43,47.
\]
Use \(p=5\). Since \(2^4\equiv1\pmod5\), for all these residues \(2^r\equiv2^3=8\equiv3\pmod5\). As \(K\equiv3\pmod5\),
\[
K2^r+1\equiv3\cdot3+1=10\equiv0\pmod5.
\]

After the preceding two steps, the only uncovered residues are the twelve residues congruent to \(1\pmod4\):
\[
1,5,9,13,17,21,25,29,33,37,41,45.
\]
They are covered as follows.

3. **The residues \(1,13,25,37\).** Use \(p=7\). Each of these residues is congruent to \(1\pmod3\). Since \(2^3\equiv1\pmod7\), it follows that \(2^r\equiv2\pmod7\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod7\),
\[
K2^r+1\equiv3\cdot2+1=7\equiv0\pmod7.
\]

4. **The residues \(9,17,33,41\).** Use \(p=17\). Each of these residues is congruent to \(1\pmod8\). Since \(2^8=256\equiv1\pmod{17}\), we have \(2^r\equiv2\pmod{17}\). Since \(K\equiv8\pmod{17}\),
\[
K2^r+1\equiv8\cdot2+1=17\equiv0\pmod{17}.
\]

5. **The residues \(5,21\).** Use \(p=257\). Since \(2^{16}=65{,}536=257\cdot255+1\), the powers of two have period dividing \(16\) modulo \(257\). Both residues are congruent to \(5\pmod{16}\), so
\[
2^r\equiv2^5=32\pmod{257}.
\]
As \(K\equiv8\pmod{257}\),
\[
K2^r+1\equiv8\cdot32+1=257\equiv0\pmod{257}.
\]

6. **The residue \(29\).** Use \(p=97\). Directly,
\[
2^{29}=97\cdot5{,}534{,}751+65,
\]
so \(2^{29}\equiv65\pmod{97}\). Since \(K\equiv94\equiv-3\pmod{97}\),
\[
K2^{29}+1\equiv(-3)\cdot65+1=-194=-2\cdot97\equiv0\pmod{97}.
\]

7. **The residue \(45\).** Use \(p=673\). Directly,
\[
2^{45}=673\cdot52{,}279{,}899{,}091+589,
\]
so \(2^{45}\equiv589\pmod{673}\). Since \(K\equiv665\equiv-8\pmod{673}\),
\[
K2^{45}+1\equiv(-8)\cdot589+1=-4711=-7\cdot673\equiv0\pmod{673}.
\]

These cases exhaust all residues \(r\in\{0,1,\ldots,47\}\). Therefore, for every positive integer \(m\), at least one of
\[
3,5,7,17,97,257,673
\]
divides \(K2^m+1\).

This divisor is always nontrivial and proper. Indeed, every number in the covering set is greater than \(1\), and every one is at most \(673<K\). On the other hand,
\[
K2^m+1>K
\]
for every positive \(m\). Hence the selected divisor \(p\) satisfies
\[
1<p<K2^m+1.
\]
Thus \(K2^m+1\) has a proper divisor and is not prime. Since this holds for every positive \(m\), and since \(K\) is odd and greater than \(1\), \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

Finally, at \(n=473{,}165\),
\[
a(n)=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}779,
\qquad
a(n)+28=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}807,
\]
and
\[
a(n)<5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783<a(n)+28.
\]
The middle integer is the Sierpiński number \(K\) just constructed. Therefore \(a(473{,}165)\) and \(a(473{,}165)+28\) are not consecutive Sierpiński numbers. This single index disproves the assertion that the pair is consecutive for every \(n\ge0\).
